prompt.context: The client is a major pharmaceutical company. It has two new drugs in development, both of which are prescription treatment-type drugs (as opposed to preventative drugs) for osteoporosis, a disease that affects older women. The development period for new drugs is ten years, but the last three years – which involve testing – consume more than half of the cost.
prompt.question: The client wants you to decide whether to test the two drugs, test one of the drugs, or to abandon the drugs altogether. Before diving into the main recommendation, the interviewer wants you to address: (1) What is the size of the potential market for osteoporosis drugs? (2) How do the markets for preventative drugs and treatment drugs differ? Then, should the client spend the money to finish developing the two drugs?

clarifying_info.q: Are the drugs treatment or preventative drugs?
clarifying_info.a: At the moment they are treatment drugs, although they could become preventative drugs in the future. The normal pattern is for drugs to come out as treatments because longer testing is required to prove value as a preventative. Consider the shorter-term possibilities as a treatment drug.

clarifying_info.q: Are there existing competitors with similar drugs already on the market?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. Both drugs are essentially the same as drugs competitors already have on the market. They are the dominant treatments of the disease.

clarifying_info.q: Are we producing generic drugs that will cost less than competitors?
clarifying_info.a: No, the client would not compete on price.

clarifying_info.q: Does anything distinguish our drugs – more effective, fewer side effects?
How well have the existing competitor drugs done?
clarifying_info.a: They have done very well. They are the dominant treatments of the disease.

clarifying_info.q: Are the competitors as large as our client?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, competitors are just as big.

framework: Likelihood of success: Is success likely in general? Do the two drugs have different chances of succeeding in testing?
Cost of test: What does testing cost? Is it the same for both drugs?

Revenue potential: What is the size of the potential market? What are side effects and delivery convenience (pill vs. shot)? How frequently is the drug sold per treatment? What is the competitive landscape?
Potential to lose market position if we do NOT test: Could staying out of this market cost us share or positioning in other markets?
Don't test: What is the cost/risk of abandoning the drugs altogether?

questions.prompt: Estimate the size of the U.S. market for osteoporosis treatment drugs.
questions.guidance: Walk through a top-down population segmentation: U.S. population → women → women over 50 (the at-risk group). Acknowledge that incidence rate and trend data would be needed to get to actual patients. Note that the market will grow as the population ages.

math.setup: U.S. population 270 million; slightly more than half are women → 135 million women. Osteoporosis primarily affects women over 50; roughly 25% of the population is over 50.
steps: 135 million women × 25% over age 50 = ~33–35 million potential customers
Next step would require incidence rate (% who develop osteoporosis) to find actual patient count
Also note trend: aging population means this segment will grow
math.answer: Approximately 33–35 million women over 50 in the U.S. are in the at-risk group; actual patient count requires incidence rate data.

questions.prompt: How does the market for a preventative drug differ from the market for a treatment drug?
questions.guidance: Consider who makes the purchase decision, what drives that decision, and how large the addressable population is. Key dimensions: randomness of disease (high-risk group vs. broad population), availability of treatment (if effective treatment exists, prevention demand falls), ease of use (pill vs. multiple pills with diet restrictions), insurance coverage, and severity of side effects.

questions.prompt: How would marketing strategy differ between a preventative drug and a treatment drug?
questions.guidance: Treatment drug: patients are already suffering and see a doctor, so doctors are the key decision-maker. Market to doctors in medical publications, emphasizing clinical effectiveness. Preventative drug: the patient has more influence because they choose whether to take a prescription preventative. Advertise broadly to the at-risk group, stressing disease consequences and ease/safety of the drug.

questions.prompt: Given the competitive landscape (competitor drugs are already the dominant treatments and essentially identical to the client's drugs, with no price or quality differentiation), should the client proceed with testing?
questions.guidance: The key insight is that with no differentiation and well-entrenched competitors of equal size, there is no clear path to stealing market share. Possible differentiation levers include advertising (driving patient preference), distribution channel advantages (hospital/insurance/drugstore contracts), and brand. The candidate should lean toward recommending against further investment, while noting the risk of being absent from an entire market category.

questions.prompt: A small West Coast start-up is developing a new type of treatment that would make the existing treatments obsolete. It is about to begin the expensive final three years of testing and is fairly certain to succeed technically if it can secure financing. What does this change about the recommendation?
questions.guidance: This new information makes investing in the existing drugs even less attractive – not only is the market crowded with identical products, but those products face obsolescence in roughly three years. The candidate should immediately recommend canceling testing of the existing drugs. Then pivot: what should the client do about the start-up? Options include: (1) develop the new drug independently – but the start-up has a seven-year head start; (2) hamper the start-up's development using market size, but this is short-lived; (3) acquire the start-up – the start-up needs capital for its final three years of testing, and the client has the resources. Acquisition lets the client leapfrog the competition in three years.

brainstorming.prompt: How would you differentiate a product that nearly duplicates an existing product in a crowded market?

categories.name: Advertising & Branding
ideas: Direct-to-consumer advertising to make patients ask for the drug by name
Physician education programs and medical publication campaigns stressing any marginal differences

categories.name: Distribution & Access
ideas: Leverage existing hospital and clinic contracts
Negotiate preferred formulary placement with insurance companies
Secure preferred shelf placement and contracts with major pharmacy chains

categories.name: Pricing & Bundling
ideas: Bundle with other drugs in the company's portfolio for institutional buyers
Offer rebate programs or patient assistance programs to drive volume

categories.name: Service & Support
ideas: Provide superior sales force support and medical liaison services
Offer disease management programs or patient adherence tools alongside the drug

recommendation: Do not invest further in testing the two existing drugs. With no differentiation from entrenched competitors of equal size, and with a new technology likely to make existing treatments obsolete in three years, the return on the testing investment is highly unfavorable.

Acquire the start-up developing the next-generation treatment. The start-up needs capital for its final three years of testing; the client has the resources. This gives the client a new drug that would leapfrog the competition and reach market in roughly three years.
risks: The start-up's new drug may face unforeseen technical or regulatory hurdles despite confidence in its approach
Acquisition price may be high if other large pharma companies also identify the start-up
Abandoning the existing drugs cedes the current osteoporosis treatment market entirely for at least three years
next_steps: Immediately cease or suspend testing of the two existing drugs to halt further cost
Approach the start-up for acquisition discussions before competitors do
Conduct due diligence on the start-up's technology, IP, development timeline, and team
Model acquisition economics vs. licensing vs. co-development options
